newsitem.title: BELGIUM: BELGIAN CEN.BANK DECLINES COMMENT ON GOLD PLANS.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN CEN.BANK DECLINES COMMENT ON GOLD PLANS.

text.p: The Belgian central bank, a pioneer in the sale of gold stocks, on Friday declined comment on German Finance Minister Theo Waigel's proposals to revalue Bundesbank gold reserves.
Central bank governor Alfons Verplaetse declined to comment, while the bank's spokesman said the bank had nothing to add to recent statements.
Verplaetse, who reduced the Belgian gold stocks to the curent 600 tonnes from 1,300 tonnes in 1990, said in February that the bank planned no further gold sales.
"I can live with our current level of gold assets," Verplaetse said in February.
He then added -- with glee -- he thought many countries were unhappy for not having done what the Belgian central bank did.
Belgium's last gold sale was in March 1996, when the bank sold 203 tonnes to an unspecified central bank.
A revaluation of its gold stocks is not an issue for the Belgian central bank, which values its gold stocks at market prices once a year at year-end.

In line with European Monetary Institute gold valuation methods for gold/ECU swaps the Belgian central bank applies the following method for determining the value: the price is either the average of the gold price at the London daily fixings in the second half of the year or the average of the two fixings in the second to last working day of the year, if the latter price is lower than the former.
"This way we are sure to take the most conservative price," a bank official told Reuters.
Waigel's plan to use the Bundesbank's gold to plug the state deficit could well have been inspired by the Belgian central bank's use of capital gains on past gold sales to reduce state debt.
In the 1996 budget, agreed last year, the Belgian government used 236 billion francs worth of central bank capital gains on gold to repay foreign currency debt.
Just like Waigel's move now, Belgium too was accused of cooking the books for EMU.
-- Geert De Clercq, Brussels Newsroom +32 2 287 6813, Fax +32 2 230 7710
